chunks: He said: Abu Ubaidullah Muhammad ibn Imran al-Marzbani reported to me, he said: Ahmad ibn Sulaiman al-Tusi narrated to me from al-Zubair ibn Bakkar, he said: Abdullah ibn Wahb narrated to me from al-Suddi, from Abd Khair, from Qubaisah ibn Jabir al-Asadi, who said:
A man came to the Commander of the Faithful Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, and questioned him about Faith. So the Imam stood up to deliver this address and said:

Praise to Allah who set the laws of Islam and made its ways easy for whoever arrived at it, and entrenched its pillars against those who attacked it, and made it an honour for whoever supported it, and a security for whoever entered it, and a guidance for whoever followed it, and an adornment for whoever adopted it, and a protection for whoever sought refuge in it, and a rope for whoever adhered to it, and a proof for whoever spoke for it, and a light for whoever sought illumination from it, and a witness for whoever disputed with it, and a victory for whoever argued with it, and a knowledge for whoever contained it, and a tradition for whoever narrated it, and a judgement for whoever judged by it, and wisdom for whoever experienced it, and intellect for whoever pondered, and understanding for whoever grasped, and certitude for whoever recognized, and insight for whoever was intent, and a sign for whoever perceived, and a lesson for whoever drew admonition, and salvation for whoever confirmed, and love from Allah for whoever reformed, and proximity for whoever anticipated, and trust for whoever entrusted, and repose for whoever handed over his affairs, and a shield for whoever endured.

Truth is its way, guidance its quality, and kindness its distinctive feature. It is the most clear path, the towering beacon, the brilliant lights, the lofty goal, the easy racetrack, the encompassing arena, the contested race, and noble horsemen. Confirming truth is its track, good deeds its beacons, jurisprudence its lights, death its goal, the world its racetrack, the Resurrection its arena, Paradise its victory, the Fire its resentment, piety its implement, and the doers of good its horsemen. Through faith one seeks guidance to good deeds, with good deeds jurisprudence is maintained, with jurisprudence death is dreaded, with death the world ends, and through the world one passes to the Resurrection, and at the Resurrection Paradise is brought close to the God-fearing, and Hellfire is revealed for the astray.

So Faith is supported by four pillars: Endurance, Certitude, Justice, and Struggle in the way of Allah. And endurance has four branches: yearning, fear, renunciation, and anticipation. Know that whoever yearns for Paradise keeps away from base desires, whoever fears the Fire abandons forbidden acts, whoever renounces the world finds ordeals easy, and whoever anticipates death hastens to charitable deeds. And certitude has four branches: discernment of intelligence, interpretation of wisdom, admonition of lessons, and the tradition of predecessors. So whoever discerns with intelligence perceives wisdom, whoever perceives wisdom understands the tradition, and whoever understands the tradition, it is as if he belonged to the predecessors. And justice has four branches: subtle insight, abundant knowledge, blossom of judgement, and garden of forbearance. So whoever has insight deserves the beauty of knowledge, whoever has knowledge knows the ways of judgement, whoever knows the ways of judgement does not go astray, and whoever is forbearing does not neglect his affairs and lives among people praised. And struggle has four branches: enjoining good, forbidding evil, truthfulness in all situations, and detestation of the impious. So whoever enjoins good strengthens the back of the believer, whoever forbids evil humbles the nose of the disbeliever, whoever is truthful in all situations fulfills what is upon him, whoever abhors the impious displays anger for Allah, and whoever displays anger for Allah the Exalted is a true believer.
This is then the definition of Faith and its pillars. The questioner said: You have indeed guided, O Commander of the Faithful, and advised. May Allah reward you the best on behalf of religion.

key_terms.الإيمان: Faith (Iman) - complete trust and belief in God, distinct from mere outward submission (Islam)
key_terms.الجهاد: Struggle (Jihad) - striving in God's way through enjoining good, forbidding evil, truthfulness, and opposing wickedness
key_terms.الصبر: Endurance/patience (Sabr) - the first pillar, subdivided into motivation, fear, renunciation, and anticipation
key_terms.العدل: Justice ('Adl) - equitable conduct based on understanding, knowledge, judgement, and forbearance
key_terms.اليقين: Certitude (Yaqin) - firm conviction based on insight, wisdom, admonition, and tradition
key_terms.دعائم: Pillars/supports - the foundational supports upon which faith is built

ai.seo_question: What are the four pillars of faith according to Imam Ali?
ai.summary: This is a famous sermon of Imam Ali ibn Abi Talib (AS) delivered in response to a man's question about the nature and definition of faith (iman). Using elaborate rhetorical parallelism, the Imam first describes Islam's blessings through a series of metaphors, then employs an equestrian metaphor comparing faith to a racecourse, and finally defines faith as resting on four pillars: endurance (sabr), certitude (yaqin), justice ('adl), and struggle (jihad), each subdivided into four branches. This sermon, delivered in Kufa to the early Muslim community, demonstrates the Imam's unparalleled eloquence and his systematic theological framework.

en.mulla-asgharali-m-m-jaffer: 3. He said: Abu Ubaidullah Muhammad ibn Imran al-Marzbani reported to me from Ahmad ibn Sulaiman al-Tusi, from al-Zubair ibn Bakkar, from Abdullah ibn Wahab, from al-Suddi, from Abd Khair, from Qubaisah ibn Jabir al-Asadi, who said:
A man visited Amirul Mu’mineen ‘Ali ibn Abi Talib, peace be upon him, and questioned him about Faith. So, Imam stood up to deliver this address:

"Praise to Allah who set the laws of Islam, and made its ways easy for whoever arrived at it, and entrenched its basis against those who came to destroy it. And made it an honour for those who supported it, and a security for those who entered it. He made it a guidance for those who followed it, and an adornment for those who adopted it. He made it a protection for those who sought refuge in it, and a strong rope for those who adhered to it. He made it a proof for those who spoke for it, a light for those who sought to be illuminated by it, a strong witness against those who disputed it, and a victory for those who argued for it. He made it a (good) knowledge for those who contained it and a (worthy) tradition for those who narrated about it. He made it the (best) basis of judgement for those who adjudged by it, (full of) wisdom for those who experienced, source of intellect for those who pondered, an understanding for those who grasped, certitude for those who recognized, an insight for those who are intent, a sign for those who perceive, an admonition for those who draw lesson, salvation for those who confirmed its truth. He made it a way of divine love for those who reformed (themselves) and a path of proximity (to Allah) for those who expected it, and a place of trust for those who entrusted. He made it a repose for those who handed over the charge of their affairs (to Allah) and a shield for those who endure.

Truth is its way, guidance its (prime) quality, kindness its distinctive feature. It is the most clear path, the towering beacon, the most brilliant light. (Using an equestrian metaphor, he said), It has the highest flag, facile racetrack, an encompassing arena, a contestant for winning the race, and noble horsemen. Confirming the truth is its track, good deeds are its beacons, learning Islam is its light, death is its flag (at the destination), the world is its racetrack, and the Day of Reckoning is its arena; and attaining Paradise its victory, and hellfire its resentment. Taqwa is its implement and people of good deeds are its horsemen. From Faith, one seeks guidance to good and righteous deeds, and with the righteous deeds, learning of Islam is (truly) maintained. And with the knowledge of Islam, death is dreaded, and with death comes the end of (life in) the world. And it is through this world (life) that one passes over to Resurrection, and it will be with the Resurrection, that Paradise will be brought close to the God-fearing, and justify hell for those who have gone astray.

So Faith is supported by four pillars: Endurance, Certitude, Justice and struggle (in the way of Allah). And endurance among them is subdivided into four branches: motivation, fear, renunciation and anticipation. Know you that one who is motivated by the yearning for Paradise keeps away from base desires, and one who fears hell abandons the forbidden acts, and one who renounces (by detachment from the) world, finds it easy to face the worldly ordeals, and who anticipates death, hastens to do charitable deeds. And certitude has four branches: intelligent discernment, wise interpretation, drawing lesson from the events, and (studying) the example of the previous generations. So, he who discerns with intelligence will be able to unravel (the secrets of) wisdom, and he who perceives wisdom understands the tradition (handed down) and for he who understands the tradition, it will be as if he belongs to the past generation. And justice has four branches: subtle insight, abundant knowledge, being sensibly judicious and drilled in patience. So he who has an insight, deserves the beauty of knowledge, and he who has knowledge, knows the ways of dispensing justice, and he who is judicious, never goes astray. And he who is patient and enduring never neglects his affairs and thus lives among the people highly appreciated. And struggle (in the way of Allah) has four branches: enjoining good, forbidding evil, being truthful in all situations, and detestation of the impious. So he who enjoins good, lends strength to the believer, and he who forbids evil earns the scorn of the unbelievers; and he who is truthful in all situations (fearlessly) judges against himself, and he who abhors the impious displays anger for the sake of Allah; and he who displays anger for His sake is a true believer.
This is then the definition of Faith and its props." The questioner rose and said: "You have indeed guided, O Amirul Mu’mineen, and advised. May Allah reward you best on behalf of Islam."
